notes: Plain definitions for terms the Sky Journeys cards and narration use (owner feedback round 1: define every technical term at first use). Each `short` is at most 25 words, original wording. Plurals (s/es, y→ies, a→ae) are matched automatically; `aliases` hold other spellings. Matching: client/src/lib/journeys/plain-language.ts findGlossaryTerms. Numbers in definitions are either definitional (unit conversions, the magnitude scale) or carry `citations`.

terms.short: The distance light travels in one year: about 9.5 trillion km. It measures distance, not time.
The tiny shift of a nearby star against far ones as Earth circles the Sun. The smaller the shift, the farther the star.
The astronomer's brightness scale. Smaller numbers are brighter; each step of 5 magnitudes is a factor of 100 in brightness.
How bright a star would look from a standard distance of about 33 light-years, so stars can be compared fairly.
The total light a star really gives off, however near or far it is. The Sun's is the usual yardstick.
The circle of sky your binoculars show at once. Its width in degrees is printed on most binoculars.
One sixtieth of a degree. The full Moon is about 30 arcminutes wide.
One sixtieth of an arcminute. The gaps in close double stars are measured in arcseconds.
Looking slightly to one side of a faint object, so its light falls on the more sensitive edge of your eye.
A recognizable star pattern that is not a whole constellation, like the Big Dipper or the Summer Triangle.
One of 88 official regions of the sky, each named after the old star figure inside it, such as Orion or Cygnus.
A loose family of stars born together from one cloud, usually a few hundred million years old or younger.
A dense ball of hundreds of thousands of very old stars, orbiting our galaxy far from its flat disk.
A loose, spread-out family of young, hot, heavy stars that formed together and are drifting apart.
Stars scattered across the sky that still travel through space together, a sign they were born as one family.
A cloud of gas and dust in space. Some glow, some reflect starlight and some block the light behind them.
A gas cloud glowing on its own because hot young stars inside energize it, like the gas in a neon sign.
A dust cloud that makes no light of its own and shines by reflecting nearby starlight, usually looking blue in photos.
A cold cloud of dust thick enough to block the stars behind it, seen as a dark patch.
A dark band of dust cutting across a galaxy or the Milky Way, blocking the light from behind.
A cloud of gas and dust where new stars are forming right now.
A newborn star cluster still wrapped in the cloud it formed from.
A star still forming: a collapsing ball of gas that is not yet hot enough in its core to fuse hydrogen.
A very young star, a few million years old at most, still shrinking and flickering on its way to adulthood.
Atoms crushed together in a star's core into heavier ones, releasing the energy that makes the star shine.
The lightest and most common element, the main fuel stars burn for most of their lives.
The second-lightest element. Stars make it by fusing hydrogen, and heavier stars later fuse it into carbon and oxygen.
The long, steady adult stage of a star's life, when it quietly fuses hydrogen in its core, as the Sun does now.
A letter code (O B A F G K M) sorting stars from hottest to coolest by the lines in their light.
Starlight spread into its rainbow of colors. Dark or bright lines in it reveal a star's makeup, temperature and motion.
The temperature scale astronomers use: degrees Celsius plus about 273. The Sun's surface is about 5,800 kelvin.
The mass of the Sun, used as the unit for weighing stars.
A small, cool star lighter than the Sun. Such stars burn their fuel so slowly that they outlive every other kind.
A star that has just run out of hydrogen in its core and is starting to swell toward becoming a giant.
An ageing star that has used up the hydrogen in its core and swollen to many times its old size, cooling to orange or red.
A settled stage for ageing giants, when they quietly fuse helium in their cores, so many share a similar brightness.
A heavy star late in life, swollen to enormous size and pouring out thousands of times the Sun's light.
The rarest, most luminous kind of supergiant: so bloated and unstable it sheds huge amounts of gas.
A very hot, heavy star that has blown away its outer hydrogen, exposing its fierce inner layers. It will likely explode.
A huge, unstable blue star that brightens and erupts unpredictably, throwing off shells of gas.
A hot star spinning so fast that it flings gas into a glowing disk around its waist.
A cool giant whose atmosphere is rich in carbon, which filters out blue light and makes it look deep red.
When a giant's churning layers carry freshly made elements, such as carbon, up from its core to its surface.
The leftover core of a Sun-like star: about Earth's size but as heavy as the Sun, slowly cooling for billions of years.
The crushed core left by a supernova: heavier than the Sun, yet only about the size of a city.
A spinning neutron star that sweeps beams of radiation past Earth like a lighthouse, many times a second.
A collapsed object whose gravity is so strong that not even light can escape it.
The glowing shell a dying Sun-like star puffs off. It has nothing to do with planets; early telescopes made them look like planets.
The explosion of a star, briefly outshining a whole galaxy of ordinary stars. Heavy stars end this way.
The expanding cloud of debris left after a star exploded.
A sudden flare-up when a white dwarf steals gas from a partner star and the gas ignites on its surface.
A steady stream of gas blowing off a star's surface into space.
A star whose brightness changes, because it pulses, erupts, or is eclipsed by a partner.
A pulsing supergiant that brightens and fades on a strict rhythm. The slower the rhythm, the more light it really gives off.
A cool red giant that slowly swells and shrinks over many months, changing brightness enormously.
A giant or supergiant that pulses with a rough, unreliable rhythm.
A star that swells and shrinks in a rhythm, getting brighter and fainter as it does.
A graph of a star's brightness over time, showing how it rises and falls.
An object whose true brightness is known, so how faint it looks tells you how far away it is.
Two stars orbiting each other, held together by gravity.
Two stars that look close together. Some orbit each other; others only line up by chance.
Two stars that only look close because they lie in nearly the same direction, at very different distances.
Two stars whose orbit we see edge-on, so they take turns passing in front of each other and the light dips.
A pair too close to split with any telescope, revealed only by the back-and-forth shifts in its spectrum.
The other star in a pair, usually the fainter one.
When one object passes in front of another and hides it, such as the Moon covering a star.
A star's slow drift across the sky as it moves through space, measured over years or centuries.
How fast a star moves toward or away from us, measured from shifts in its spectrum.
Several telescopes linked to act as one giant one, sharp enough to measure star sizes or split very close pairs.
A planet orbiting a star other than the Sun.
A ring of dust and rubble around a star, left over from building planets.
Gas falling onto a star or other object, often swirling into a disk as it goes.
Light with longer waves than red, invisible to the eye. It passes through dust and shows cool things.
Light with shorter waves than violet, invisible to the eye. Hot stars pour out lots of it.
Very energetic light, invisible to the eye, given off by gas at millions of degrees.
Gas whose atoms have had electrons knocked off by strong light; when the electrons return, the gas glows.
Our home galaxy, and the faint band of light it makes across the sky because we see its disk from inside.
The flat, spinning pancake of stars, gas and dust where the Sun and most young stars of our galaxy live.
The huge, thin sphere of old stars and globular clusters surrounding a galaxy's flat disk.
The crowded, rounded swarm of stars at the center of a spiral galaxy.
A rich patch of the Milky Way where we look through gaps in the dust into crowds of distant stars.
A galaxy shaped like a flat disk with curving arms of young stars and gas around a central bulge.
A smooth, egg-shaped galaxy of mostly old stars, with little gas left to make new ones.
A small galaxy, often orbiting a larger one like a moon around a planet.
Our neighborhood of galaxies: the Milky Way, Andromeda, the Triangulum Galaxy and dozens of small ones.
Caused by gravity pulling harder on the near side of an object than the far side, stretching or tearing it.
A star in an old cluster that looks too young and blue, probably made when two stars merged or swapped gas.
Containing few elements heavier than helium: a sign of a very old star, born before such elements were common.
The point in the sky straight above your head.
Close enough to the celestial pole that it never sets from your location, circling the pole all night.
